meta.source_system: Lights Out puzzle (Tiger Electronics handheld, 1995; toggle rule and all-off goal, rules public), transcribed as the 3x3 deterministic variant: 9 toggle buttons, no randomness collected, no score
meta.source_citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lights_Out_(game)): Gameplay ('Pressing any of the lights will toggle it and the four adjacent lights.'; 'The goal of the puzzle is to switch all the lights off, preferably in as few button presses as possible.'), Strategy ('the order in which the lights are pressed does not matter, as the result will be the same'; 'pressing a light twice is equivalent to not pressing it at all'); Jaap's Puzzle Page "Lights Out" (www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/lights.htm), the rules page Wikipedia cites for the game: 'By pressing a button, its light and those of the (non-diagonally) adjacent buttons will change (switch on if it was off, and vice versa).'; board-size variant boundary: Wikipedia ('The game consists of a 5 by 5 grid of lights'; Merlin 'with similar rules on a 3 by 3 grid'; 'Lights Out Cube (six 3x3 faces with effects across edges)'). Per-rule citations in meta.rules_with_citations; per-edge generating rules in meta.edge_rule_tags; the nine toggle masks in meta.toggle_masks.
meta.state_encoding: state = 9 bits = 9 lamps; lamp i = 3*row + col (row, col counted from the top-left), bit i = lamp i with 1=on, 0=off; ALL 512 bit patterns are valid configurations (no padding states -- toggle-matrix rank 9, see meta.toggle_matrix_rank)
meta.semantics_class: position-button: the nine actions are the nine board buttons at fixed positions; a board symmetry moves buttons with the cells, so true board symmetries are explicit-caliber claims with per-element button renamings; the fixed reading (buttons pinned) is the naive contrast. XOR-translations of the lamp vector (e.g. the all-lamps complement) keep every button name and hold under the fixed caliber
meta.reward_rule: all zero by design: the source game has no score (see meta.rules_with_citations R6); the win condition is recorded in meta.win_condition, not as a per-edge reward (same all-zero convention as tcp/dhcp/imap)
meta.win_condition: all nine lamps off (state 0) -- 'The goal of the puzzle is to switch all the lights off' (Wikipedia Gameplay); the device does not lock on winning, so state 0 is an ordinary state of the transition system and goals=[] in this model

rules_with_citations.rule: pressing a button toggles it and its orthogonal (non-diagonal) neighbors; on the 3x3 board a corner button toggles 3 lamps, an edge button 4, the center button 5 -- the toggle set is always the button itself plus its in-grid orthogonal neighbors (out-of-grid neighbors are ignored)
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", Gameplay: 'Pressing any of the lights will toggle it and the four adjacent lights.' (the 5x5 wording; on the 3x3 board the four adjacent DIRECTIONS shrink to the in-grid ones); Jaap's Puzzle Page "Lights Out" (www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/lights.htm), 'By pressing a button, its light and those of the (non-diagonally) adjacent buttons will change (switch on if it was off, and vice versa).'

rules_with_citations.rule: the goal of the puzzle is to switch all the lights off; the all-off configuration (state 0) is the win condition
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", Gameplay: 'The goal of the puzzle is to switch all the lights off, preferably in as few button presses as possible.'; Jaap's Puzzle Page "Lights Out" (www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/lights.htm), 'Given a pattern of lights, you have to switch them all off by pressing the correct buttons.'

rules_with_citations.rule: the order in which buttons are pressed does not matter -- the resulting configuration depends only on WHICH buttons were pressed an odd number of times
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", Strategy: 'the order in which the lights are pressed does not matter, as the result will be the same'; Jaap's Puzzle Page "Lights Out" (www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/lights.htm), 'the order that the moves are performed is unimportant (i.e. the puzzle positions form an Abelian group)'

rules_with_citations.rule: pressing the same button twice returns to the previous configuration, so no button ever needs to be pressed more than once (toggle algebra over GF(2))
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", Strategy: 'pressing a light twice is equivalent to not pressing it at all'; Jaap's Puzzle Page "Lights Out" (www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/lights.htm), 'Since pressing a button twice will not change anything, a button need only be pressed at most once.'

rules_with_citations.rule: NOT COLLECTED: the starting board is set to a random pattern or a stored pattern; the model here is the full 512-state transition system and the initial setup is outside the deterministic FSM semantics
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", Gameplay: 'When the game starts, a random number or a stored pattern of these lights is switched on.' -- randomness is outside the deterministic FSM semantics; recorded, not repaired

rules_with_citations.rule: the game has no score; 'as few button presses as possible' is advice about solutions, not a numeric payoff, so the reward layer is all zero by design
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", Gameplay: 'preferably in as few button presses as possible' -- recorded, not turned into a reward; same all-zero reward convention as the tcp/dhcp/imap cases

rules_with_citations.rule: VARIANT BOUNDARY: this case is the 3x3 board; the Tiger Electronics original is 5x5
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", 'Lights Out is an electronic game released by Tiger Electronics in 1995.'; 'The game consists of a 5 by 5 grid of lights.'; the 3x3 board is the classic smaller variant of the same rules: 'Merlin, a similar electronic game, was released by Parker Brothers in the 1970s with similar rules on a 3 by 3 grid'; 'Lights Out Cube (six 3x3 faces with effects across edges)'; Jaap's Puzzle Page "Lights Out" (www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/lights.htm), on the reissued Merlin: 'They are now exactly the same as the standard Lights Out, i.e. each button press changes its own light as well as the orthogonally adjacent ones. It has simply become a 3x3 Lights out.'

rules_with_citations.rule: play itself is deterministic: a press always toggles its cross exactly, with no randomness (the initial-board randomization of R5 is the only stochastic step, and it is not collected)
rules_with_citations.citation: consequence of R1 as stated by Wikipedia "Lights Out (game)", and Jaap's Puzzle Page "Lights Out" (www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/lights.htm),  (a press changes exactly its cross; nothing else happens)

toggle_masks.layout: toggle_masks.masks[a] = the bit mask (int) of the lamps that button a toggles (bit i = lamp i); toggle_masks.cells[a] = the same masks as cell-index lists; button a always toggles lamp a itself (rule R1)

edge_rule_tags.layout: edge_rule_tags.values[s] is a 9-character string, character a = the generating rule of edge (s, action a); T = the toggle rule R1. Every edge of this model is generated by R1 (the toggle cross), so every character is T; there are no padding self-loops and no other generating rules

transcription_notes: scope: 3x3 board, 9 two-state lamps, 9 buttons; the deterministic toggle core of Lights Out (rule R1) with the initial-board randomization NOT collected (rule R5) -- randomness is not part of the deterministic FSM semantics, per the court's not-collected discipline (same pattern as mini2048's random-spawn rule).

VARIANT BOUNDARY (rule R7): the 3x3 board; the Tiger original is 5x5. Every cited rule sentence is size-independent except the grid size; the 3x3 lineage runs through Merlin's reissued Magic Square ('exactly the same as the standard Lights Out ... a 3x3 Lights out', Jaap's page) and the Lights Out Cube's 3x3 faces.
actions: the nine buttons indexed by board position 0..8 row-major (button a sits on lamp a) -- action indices are positional data, not a court choice.
encoding: state = 9 bits = 9 lamps; bit i = lamp i, 1=on, 0=off. ALL 512 bit patterns are valid configurations.

no padding states: the 9x9 toggle matrix over GF(2) has rank 9 (asserted by this generator on every run), so every configuration is reachable from the all-off state; every state has 9 distinct active successors (zero self-loops: each toggle mask contains its own button bit) and no two states share a row. Contrast mini2048, where 175 of 256 states are padding. Consequence: the trivial positive control here is NOT a padding swap -- see the complement note below.

rewards: all zero by design (rule R6) -- the source game has no score; the win condition (all lamps off, state 0) is recorded in meta.win_condition as a terminal property and the device does not lock on winning, so state 0 is an ordinary state of the transition system. The adjudication therefore runs entirely on the transition layer (same all-zero convention as tcp/dhcp/imap).

explicit caliber note: a board symmetry moves the buttons with the cells (rotating the board clockwise turns the top-left button into the top-right button); rho(identity)=id while rho(rot90)!=id, so no single action_map can serve a whole closed group. Since 2026-11-04 the engine's group format accepts semantics.action_maps (one bijection per element, parallel to elements, homomorphism-law checked at load); each explicit group file here declares the per-element maps of its own elements, and meta.per_element_action_maps holds the full derivation (exhaustively derived over all 9! = 362880 button permutations, unique per element, asserted on every run).

complement positive control (deviation note, ruled 2026-11-04 during case engineering: faithful transcription outranks control-form symmetry): because toggling is XOR, complementing the whole board (pi(s) = 511 XOR s) commutes with every button press and keeps every button name, so it is a genuine symmetry under the fixed caliber; it plays the role mini2048's padding swap plays there (this case has no padding states to swap). Filed as g3_complement.

structural observation (machine-asserted on every run): the complement map commutes with every element of the board group D4, so the group generated by the two is the direct product D4 x C2 of order 16 -- filed as g5_d4_x_c2. Geometric symmetry and toggle-algebra symmetry are independent here and their product is a symmetry; the model's full automorphism inventory is larger still and is NOT claimed by any group file (every group here is derived, closed, and machine-asserted; no group file claims to be the full automorphism group).
